claims.text: The target alloy has an FCC/B2 eutectic phase constitution.
Before aging, the alloy is fine-grained and contains dispersed B2 ordered domains in an FCC matrix.
Intermediate thermal aging causes LCOs to coalesce into percolating networks along phase boundaries.
Percolating B2-like LCO networks at phase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation cross-slip.
Suppression of cross-slip by LCO networks forces dislocations into planar slip.
Planar slip produces localized shear bands that promote brittle fracture.
During intermediate aging, constituent solutes segregate locally to form extended LCOs at phase boundaries rather than discrete precipitates.
The LCO networks increase the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion.
At higher aging temperatures, LCOs dissolve or fragment into discrete particles.
Dissolution or fragmentation of LCO networks restores dislocation cross-slip and alloy ductility.
Aging produces a non-monotonic ductility response consisting of high initial ductility, brittle failure at intermediate temperatures, and recovered ductility at higher temperatures.
The brittle regime will exhibit planar dislocation slip bands.
The recovered ductile regime will exhibit wavy slip associated with active cross-slip.
Classical grain-boundary embrittlement through impurity segregation and grain coarsening is absent or negligible in the specified operating regime.
The embrittlement regime is bounded by temperatures at which LCOs are stable as continuous networks but have not yet dissolved.
Temperatures at which grain coarsening dominates or impurity segregation becomes the primary driver lie outside the proposed embrittlement regime.
LCO evolution occurs faster than grain coarsening in the intermediate-temperature regime.
The absence of percolating phase-boundary LCO networks during the brittle regime would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Observation of wavy slip despite the presence of LCOs would falsify the proposed cross-slip-suppression mechanism.
